articles.title: Security-development nexus
articles.content: PAKISTAN can’t achieve sustained economic growth by treating security as a separate problem for the security apparatus to handle while economists focus on investment, exports, productivity and fiscal reform. Insecurity destroys the very conditions on which economic development depends, while development strengthens the foundations of security. Our crisis makes this nexus impossible to ignore. For decades, discussions on investment, production, growth, and development have largely focused on economic policies while underestimating the non-economic environment in which they operate. Yet, security of life and property, political stability, rule of law, judicial independence, federal-provincial coordination, accountability, and regional peace directly affect economic outcomes. Unless these improve, returns from economic reforms will remain below potential. Increasing militancy and Pakistan’s top position on the Global Terrorism Index 2026 are damaging lives and economic prospects. The recentattackon a police compound in Kohat, in which 37 people, including military personnel, were killed, received international coverage. Foreign business people and executives reportedly cancelled planned visits, while travel advisories issued by several governments can discourage their nationals from visiting Pakistan. In 2025, TTP attacks in KP and BLA strikes in Balochistan caused hundreds of casualties among security personnel. The past decade’s trend shows that terrorism is no longer episodic. It is a structural constraint on investment, trade, tourism, development and employment. The origins of the TTP challenge go back several decades. Pakistan’s decision in the 1980s to align with the US in opposing the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan had consequences beyond the immediate strategic goal. The proliferation of arms and drugs, sectarian violence, growth of militant groups and the spread of extremist ideologies created a social and institutional environment that facilitated terrorism in Pakistan. After the Soviets left Afghanistan, Pakistan became involved in efforts to shape a political settlement among Afghan factions. The failure of power-sharing arrangements and the ensuing civil war led to the emergence of the Taliban, who captured Kabul in 1996. Pakistan supported their regime. But 9/11 fundamentally altered the situation. Pakistan joined the global campaign against terrorism, itself becoming a major target. When the US decided to leave Afghanistan, Pakistan played an important role in theDoha process.The Ashraf Ghani government’s collapse in 2021 and the Taliban’sreturnled to expectations that cross-border terrorism would decline. Instead, the TTP, now equipped with modern weapons left behind by Nato forces, intensified their attacks. The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security. Diplomatic efforts involving China, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye have not produced a durable solution. Insecurity along the western frontier has disrupted bilateral trade, imposing costs on manufacturers, traders and transport operators, especially in KP and Balochistan. Security and commerce are now directly linked. Balochistan poses a different but equally serious challenge. It has seen a sharp escalation in asymmetric warfare and insurgency. Highways, railways, bridges, gas pipelines, electricity transmission lines, and other infrastructure have been targeted. Mine workers, labourers from other provinces and government officials have been attacked or abducted. In places, the state’s administrative presence and writ have been weakened. The economic consequences are immediate. Chinese nationals and companies in Pakistan need extensive security. Attacks on Chinese citizens in Karachi, Dasu and elsewhere have led to concerns in Beijing and slowed some CPEC-related activities. Gwadar’s industrial potential remains largely unrealised, partly because Chinese companies are reluctant to deploy personnel in insecure conditions. An industrial zone won’t flourish when investors can’t operate confidently. Security operations alone can’t resolve Balochistan’s problem. Kinetic action is necessary against militants but must be accompanied by development. Balochistan suffers from serious deficits in education, health, clean water, infrastructure, employment and private investment. When economic opportunities are few, grievances become a source of recruitment for insurgent groups. So the province needs not just security spending but also a development strategy to create jobs, boost local institutions, and ensure communities see tangible benefits from Balochistan’s natural resources and strategic location. Regional instability adds to the problem. Disruption of trade with Iran and closure or restriction of border crossings such as Chaman have hurt exporters and communities that rely on cross-border commerce. Clearly, peace is not just a diplomatic aim; it is an economic asset. Pakistan must use its diplomatic capital to promote regional economic integration. Better ties with Afghanistan, structured dialogue with India, stable relations with Iran, and expanded links with Central Asian states can enlarge its economic space. Afghanistan, Iran, north India, and Central Asia can be important markets for Pakistani goods and services. Gwadar could become a transshipment and logistics gateway for landlocked Central Asian economies, generating transit revenues and creating opportunities for Pakistani exporters. Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan offer markets that Pakistan has so far penetrated modestly. Regional connectivity can revive projects such as the Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline, TAPI, and CASA, subject to their political, financial, commercial, and security feasibility. Greater regional trade will create demand for transport, logistics, warehousing, banking, insurance, IT and manufacturing. It will create jobs and give border communities greater economic stake in stability. None of this means that economic reforms should wait for peace. Quite the contrary. Fiscal reform, energy sector restructuring, taxation, deregulation, privatisation, export diversification, human capital development and institutional reform must continue uninterrupted. But they must be supported by steps that reduce the security premium imposed on economic activity. Security and development are two sides of the same national strategy. Insecurity raises transaction costs, discourages investment, destroys infrastructure, disrupts trade, deters foreign personnel and limits employment. Lack of economic opportunity, weak institutions and regional isolation can deepen the conditions in which insecurity flourishes. The goal should be to create an economy in which security, development and opportunity reinforce each other. Military capability can suppress threats. But only sustained economic development, effective institutions, political stability and regional peace can remove many of the conditions that allow those threats to regenerate. Our choice is not between security and development. The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security. Until that nexus becomes the organising principle of policy, economic reforms will operate below their potential and Pakistan will remain vulnerable to cycles of instability, low investment and weak growth. The writer is a former State Bank governor.
articles.author: Ishrat Husain

articles.title: Off to elect another people
articles.content: THE embattled prime minister of Israel has sworn to strip the citizenship of two Jewish filmmakers whose celebrated documentary has exposed the targeted genocide of Palestinian civilians carried out with impunity by the IDF. Journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have won standing ovations in the West for their film NAZA. The rule, Benjamin Netanyahu said, would apply to anyone who insults Israel’s military. Meanwhile, the fascism-hugging president of the US is busy doing what he can to try to strip those of citizenship and voting rights who are least likely to vote for his party. If he doesn’t win the midterms, he could be impeached. India’s ruling party, struggling to mask its old inspiration from the Nazis, has devised its own methods of stripping the citizenship rights of millions. According to a slew of reports, the BJP government is leaning on its chosen three-member election commission to deregister millions with a view to contriving state victories for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party. Bertolt Brecht’s satirical call to elect another people since the people had lost the confidence of the government has become ominously and palpably real. Coordinated moves by the three countries are linked by a quirk of fate in a post-Cold War bond. The rogue measures are not going unchallenged. A groundswell of protests primarily by students and unemployed youth is spreading across India against what reports have identified as the plundering of democracy in the country. New York’s Zohran Mamdani, Israel’s filmmakers and India’s Cockroach Janta Party are leading the pushback. The Indian protesters are directly accusing Modi’s handpicked three-member election commission of effectively changing poll verdicts, most recently in Bihar and West Bengal, by manipulating electoral rolls and surrendering the election commission’s neutral platform to the ruling party. The subversion is part of a global fraying of the lipstick on the pig, the ideological sleight of hand that was used to paint bourgeois democracies as enticing options against communist hardships. The moment the Soviet Union collapsed, however, the West’s definition of democracy itself took on a new life. It would henceforth be ‘free-market democracy’. Now that veneer, too, has blown away to herald raw plunder, assassinations, kidnappings and what leftist analysts have called ‘AI feudalism’. As the lipstick fades, big-power global rivalries deepen with unabashed candour. The West sought to keep up the pretence of supporting democracy, even though the fangs were out against elected and independent-minded leaders — for instance, in Iran in 1953 or Chile in 1973. Drooling at the promise of the American century, a clutch of former allies of the USSR were reduced to rubble. Yevgeny Primakov was the head of the KGB’s foreign intelligence unit when the USSR collapsed. He became Russia’s foreign minister and subsequently rose to become prime minister. Primakov moved to staunch the Russian haemorrhage caused by the chasm between Mikhail Gorbachev and Boris Yeltsin. The Russia-India-China (RIC) grouping was his brainchild, but he was already late since the US-Israel-India group was installed more swiftly. For Indian ideologues, who were regarded as Western catspaws during the Cold War, the alignment with Israel under the false pretence of democratic camaraderie was a windfall. The BJP gained most from the turn of events, though the Congress had its own pro-West ideologues licking their chops. As the lipstick fades, big-power global rivalries deepen with unabashed candour. As capitalism struggled to breathe sans the Red Terror as its ruse, the fangs could barely be hidden. During the Cold War (roughly 1945-1991), capitalist democracies — particularly in Western Europe and North America — faced a powerful ideological rival in global communism. To prove that capitalism was the superior system for the working class, many Western nations built robust welfare states. They invested heavily in public healthcare and education, strong labour unions and worker protections, high progressive taxation to fund social safety nets, and affordable housing and infrastructure. Most analysts have concluded that the systemic threat of communism acted as a ‘regulatory check’ on raw capitalism, forcing it to present a more compassionate, egalitarian face to prevent domestic socialist revolutions. Once the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, critics and economists argue, this pressure disappeared. With no competing global model, a more aggressive, unregulated version of capitalism led by neoliberalism gained dominant global traction. Whether it involves winning elections by waging brutal wars or carrying out genocide, or stripping voters of their rights, the trigger is capitalism’s inability to leave its fate to the voting masses. While democracy promises power to the many, its mechanisms can be co-opted by the few to maintain control. Some regimes maintain the outward appearance of democracy — such as holding regular elections — while systematically eroding democratic institutions from within. This dynamic is often referred to as a ‘hybrid regime’ or ‘competitive authoritarianism’. Ruling elites use legal frameworks, regulatory bodies, and gerrymandering to tilt the playing field in their favour, making it incredibly difficult for opposition forces to compete fairly. It’s evident in India, as in the US or Israel — the post-Cold War ‘democratic allies’ — that campaign financing, lobbying, and the influence of wealthy donors mean that policy decisions really reflect the interests of economic elites rather than those of the average voter. All three countries have used religion to manufacture consent. This is beginning to create a disconnect in which citizens feel their vote carries no real weight in policy outcomes. The Jantar Mantar protests in Delhi are a clear aspect of this churning. The protesters are well aware that elites consolidate control over media landscapes or leverage algorithms and disinformation to shape public perception. By controlling the narrative, they can manufacture consent or distract the public from systemic issues. Donald Trump’s threat from the UN platform to murder 91 million Iranians, and the Indian election commission’s removal of 130m names from electoral rolls in the last nine months, are shared responses to their fraying economies’ growing need to dump democratic pretence all over again. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: A bailout state?
articles.content: THE country’s external liquidity rests shakily on the two crutches of endless IMF loans and rollovers of patron-state deposits. Both carry high costs — economic and political. Our rulers entice patron states to bankroll a near-bankrupt state via its geopolitical, not economic, value. Rulers exploit both for personal, not public, gains. They court patrons well, but turn patronage into public progress poorly and personal profits ably. So, our growth spurts are all import-led rather than export-led. We spend dollars faster than we earn and court crises. We recover by choking growth instead of increasing it alongside exports. We have had several chances but have squandered most of them. Musharraf squandered the biggest one this century. He ruled the longest, with the deep state and opposition under his thumb, and gained over $45bn in US aid, debt relief, FDI, and portfolio inflows after 9/11. Yet, a strong export base eluded him. Inflows fuelled consumption, imports, and property binges and bubbles; volatile portfolio funds and domestically focused FDI later led to outflows. They initially kept the rupee high, hurting exports. Their value doubled, but value-added dawdled and the export-GDP ratio fell below 1990s levels. A record current account deficit of 8.2 per cent of GDP in 2008 led to a big crisis. Bad security policies fuelled two conflicts that still hurt progress. The PPP cut the deficit. But energy woes, insecurity, ineptitude and failed reforms reduced growth. Later, CPEC provided over $20 billion for energy and roads. This eased energy gaps, but the PML-N failed to build a durable export base. An expensive rupee led to an import surge and a current account deficit of about 6pc by 2018. The PTI had brought it down to 0.6pc by 2021 and managed the Covid phase well. But the Covid stimulus raised imports as exports lagged. The deficit rose to 4.6pc in 2022, partly due to global price shocks and political turmoil. So, the PML-N bequeathed a crisis to the PTI only to inherit one back, karma-style. We spend dollars faster than we earn and court crises. Import-led growth led to dollar crunches. Instead of curbing crises, high reserves made them more likely as rulers increased imports to fuel growth. Their frequency and common causes could have taught the current rulers how to avert such crises. But they are as clueless about them as they are about regular floods, even though such crises can be foreseen and forestalled. This is worse than incompetence; it shows wilful neglect. They cause and gain from such crises. The people are worse off now. As CPEC flows shrank, we courted IMF loans and state deposits, which ballooned from 36pc of the State Bank’s reserves in 2016, when deposits were only $700 million, to nearly 600pc in early 2023. About $11bn in IMF debt, $8bn in Saudi deposits and $4bn in Chinese deposits together still exceed even our highest-ever SBP reserves of $21bn. We are the most persistent user of both crutches over time, and we now have the second-most such deposits and the third-most IMF debt globally. They are on top of an external debt of over $80bn. Unlike that debt, they don’t fund projects or jobs directly, earn no direct revenue to pay the interest and are taken only due to a dollar crunch. Even these crutches may not carry the weight of our follies, so we now eye a $10bn lifeline from our oldest but most fickle patron — the US. Bangladesh, once our lesser half, has no such deposits, and its IMF debt is only 13pc of reserves as its $48bn exports mock our $30bn levels. Such crutches hurt. The PML-N and PTI both ignited growth spurts as reserves peaked. Despite higher SBP reserves now, this set-up hasn’t changed outcomes, given the nature of its reserve cushion. The IMF keeps us on a leash, and patron-state deposits can be recalled quickly (as in the UAE case), unlike flows with longer, fi_xed return dates. So, even patronage quality has fallen: from post-9/11 aid and debt relief to CPEC flows to harsh loans and fickle deposits. We now build reserves precariously rather than finance them prudently or earn them creatively. After four years, this set-up boasts only stabilisation and opaque foreign forays. But as a strong export base and growth elude it, stabilisation is really stagnation. Foreign forays are sucking us into endless wars, jeopardising our own security for the sake of others. We face two risky paths: hobble on with slow growth and risk unrest, or rush recklessly into import-led growth to court a dollar crisis and unrest. With no major investments here even from the patrons it serves loyally, only the two crutches prop up a bailout state. How long will its weak life jackets keep it afloat? The writer has a PhD in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots-to-senior-level experience across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: What a shame
articles.content: SOME emotions have become too complex. Maybe, they always were. Take shame, for instance: feeling shame for something personal you can’t control, like physical ability or appearance, is usually discouraged. However, the absence of shame over a character flaw or harmful action is frowned upon, and rightly so. Victim shaming also takes the form of stigmatisation, but that is a topic for another day. For now, I am fascinated by a recent New Yorker headline about the lack of shame and how it affects democracy. At first, it seemed like a stretch, but come to think of it, politics is a behavioural science. At home, a social media meme keeps resurfacing, even as the man who gave it new currency keeps being discredited: “koi sharm hoti hai, koi haya hoti hai” (“there’s something called shame and decency”). The lack of both in not just the political class but also in many quarters that wield power and their camp followers is not only harming democracy, it is also undermining the concept of accountability, which has to be at the core of all human endeavours and systems, especially those that pretend to be representative. A social contract, whether formalised in a constitution or codified in tradition, will be stymied if it relies solely on formal legal checks and balances, because a bit of ‘shame and decency’ will not only curb harmful actions, it will also save millions in litigation and prevent millions from losing trust in the system. Official vehicles and residences for state functionaries have long been the subject of civil service reform studies and will continue to be, as extensions and consultancies are provided to retired officials so that they can retain vehicles and refuse to vacate residences they have proposed monetising. The discussion has been elevated to include planes for public office holders. The absence of shame is hurting the world. Both the optics and economics of maintaining and operating aircraft at state expense for public officials in debt-burdened countries are problematic. One argument calls for a fuller account of the impact of the time saved. The security angle is even more irksome, as those endangering security are, or have been, state-sponsored at some point. The air around the topic grows more turbulent when these aircraft are (mis)used for private travel. The respective courtiers’ justifications keep absurdity levels high. In the recent case involving Punjab chief executive Maryam Nawaz, she was first heard telling critics off, asserting that no activity by a chief minister is purely personal, thus implying that important provincial business was conducted alongside her daughter’s graduation ceremony in London. Then her spokespersons announced that she had paid for the trip out of her own pocket. How about the aircraft’s depreciation, since these aircraft come with flight-hour limits? The most vocal critics of the chief minister’s flight of fancy are from the PTI — the same people who went blue in the face explaining that Imran Khan’s helicopter jaunts between Prime Minister House and Banigala were cheaper than a taxi ride. But expecting shame and decency from someone who thinks women should be discouraged from riding bikes because he believes they are “horrible drivers” is like asking a jellyfish to show spine. People who gifted back hundreds of millions of repatriated pounds in a UK money-laundering case to a criminal have the temerity to ask “koi sharm hoti hai…” ‘Honour’ is another word that needs careful handling. In the hands of ruffians, when it is confined to the female body, it becomes a tool for ‘honour’ killings. When practised by societies that encourage decency, a sense of honour calls on people in positions of power and responsibility to beg forgiveness and/ or resign from office. In certain cultures, officials who lose face take the extreme step. The world is regressing. One hopes it’s a phase that will pass. At the UN, we have heard of antics such as tearing up speeches, aiming shoes at the rostrum, and marathon addresses. But for the chiefs of the ‘shameless brigade’ to threaten the annihilation of a 91-million-strong ‘Islamic Republic’ and to gloat over a prototype gadget used in targeted killings reflects not only on these individuals but also on the systems that elevate them to positions of power and on their beneficiaries. The absence of shame is hurting the world, indeed. Meanwhile, back home, tax evaders, money launderers, rent-seekers, and shady characters continue their pilgrimages. The poet had lamented: “Kaaba kis munh say jao gey Ghalib/ sharm tum ko magar nahin aati” (“What face will you show in Kaaba/ but you’re shameless”). Those feeling left out should find solace in a translated Sindhi proverb: “kings are those unburdened by shame.” The writer is a poet. His latest publication is a collection of satire essays titled Rindana.
articles.author: Shahzad Sharjeel

articles.title: Terror and politics
articles.content: THE KP government is stuck in an unenviable spot. On one hand, the chief minister has taken it upon himself to keep the PTI alive and relevant, by channelling the considerable public sympathy behind it into tangible street power. On the other, he must lead a fightback against the resurgent wave of terrorism in his province, where casualties keep mounting. There is no easy choice for someone who is a provincial chief executive as well as a political leader; in fact, there is no choice at all. On Sunday, a day after he hadannouncedputting off the opposition’s planned protest march to Islamabad, Chief Minister Sohail Afridi visited Dera Ismail Khan to check in with those wounded in a deadly gun-and-bombattackin Darazinda over the weekend. The attack targeted a police and customs check-post and killed at least 12; militants then fired on an ambulance carrying the victims, killing two rescue workers. Accompanied by his predecessor, Ali Amin Khan Gandapur, he asked for his province’s input to be incorporated into the national counterterrorism policy, so it could “reflect the ground realities”. “Peace cannot be established without taking the people of KP into confidence,” he said. Mr Afridi complained about the non-provision of modern weapons and equipment from the centre despite payments being made. Unfortunately, he could not steer clear of politics and accused “some elements” in the federal government of polarising the country, while daring them to make good on the threat to impose governor’s rule in KP. Federal ministersrespondedon Monday, slamming the PTI government for “failing to provide leadership, resources or power” to the security forces. “If Pakistan is burning in the fire of terrorism, it is because of KP’s incompetent leadership,” the minister of state for interior remarked, sitting alongside the information minister. The state minister also accused the provincial government of having “a soft attitude” on Afghanistan. The information minister, meanwhile, branded the PTI the ‘B team’ of the banned TTP. “You will now have to decide if you are with Pakistan or with Afghanistan,” he added. This is extremely poor leadership and statesmanship from top-level leaders at a time when national unity is needed. Pakistan’s fight against violent extremism long predates the current crisis, and it is deeply unfortunate and disingenuous to cast it as a problem created solely by a single political party. That said, the KP government must demonstrate far greater responsibility in meeting the governance challenges it faces. The chief minister cannot lead a political movement at a time when citizens are dying on an almost daily basis. There is an urgent need to tone down the rhetoric and tackle terrorism as a collective challenge for both the affected provinces and the federation.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Watching the glaciers
articles.content: THE latest signs from Pakistan’s mountains are worrying. Suparco says the number of unfrozen glacial lakes it observed rose from 40 in early July to 105 in August, while some were larger than previously recorded. Not every thawing lake poses the same danger. But when a lake grows unusually large, it can put greater pressure on the loose rock and debris holding back its waters, increasing the risk of a glacial lake outburst flood. Hence, satellite monitoring is invaluable, particularly in remote mountain areas. Yet it can only tell part of the story. To know how dangerous a lake really is, experts also need information about its depth, the strength of the natural barrier around it, the condition of nearby glaciers and local weather patterns. Hanging glaciers, which can suddenly collapse and send ice or debris into a lake, present another danger that cannot always be properly understood from satellite images alone. Cloud cover can also obscure the view, as Suparco itself has noted. Pakistan must, therefore, move beyond simply counting and mapping glacial lakes. It needs to know which ones pose the greatest threat, and why. This means connecting what is seen from space with what scientists find on the ground. When satellite images show a lake expanding rapidly, it should lead to closer field checks involving Suparco, Wapda, universities, meteorological experts and the provincial disaster authorities. Their findings should be brought together in one system showing which lakes are growing, which natural barriers may be weakening, and which villages, roads or other infrastructure lie downstream. Experts have warned that agencies often work separately and that important information about glaciers and local conditions remains missing. With more than 13,000 glaciers, Pakistan cannot study each one in equal detail. Nor does it need to. Satellite monitoring can help identify the lakes that deserve the closest attention, allowing limited scientific resources to be used where the danger is greatest. The jump from 40 to 105 unfrozen lakes should, therefore, be seen as more than another warning about climate change. It is also a test of whether Pakistan can turn the information it already has into practical knowledge — and use that knowledge before a dangerous lake becomes a disaster.
articles.author: Editorial
